docs.title: 1.1.1 What is a real-time system?
docs.text:
A real-time system is a computing system designed to perform specific tasks within the specified/defined time limits (deadlines), ensuring that responses are delivered when they are needed. In such systems, producing the correct result in not enough, the result must also be available by the required time. For example, a robot's collision avoidance system must detect an obstacle and respond quickly enough to prevent a collision. Producing the correct response too late may still result in failure.

In ordinary computing, we are often mainly interested in whether a program produces the correct output. In real-time computing, the program must also produce its output within a specified timing constraint.

Let's consider a mobile robot approaching an obstacle. To avoid a collision, the robot must:

  1. Read information from its sensors.
  2. Determine whether an obstacle is present.
  3. Decide whether it needs to stop.
  4. Send the appropriate command to its motors.

If the robot makes the correct decision but responds too late, it may collide with the obstacle. Therefore, producing the correct decision is not sufficient. The decision must also arrive in time.

This illustrates an essential principle of real-time computing: both the result and its timing determine whether an operation is successful.

Key concept

Real-time correctness = Correct result + Correct timing

A real-time system must satisfy both its functional requirements (what it should do) and its timing requirements (when it should do it).

docs.title: 1.1.2 Why is real-time operation important in robotics?
docs.text:
Robots continuously interact with their physical surroundings. They receive information through sensors, process that information, and perform actions using actuators. Since the physical environment continues to change while the robot is processing information, delays can affect how accurately, efficiently, or safely the robot operates.

Examples of events requiring timely responses include:

  • mobile robot approaching an obstacle
  • robotic arm reaching its target position
  • motor rotating faster than its commanded speed
  • sensor detecting an unexpected change
  • robot receiving an emergency stop signal

The time available to respond depends on the particular task and its operating conditions.

docs.title: Example 1: Mobile robot obstacle detection
docs.text:
Imagine a mobile robot moving toward a wall. The robot uses a distance sensor to detect obstacles and a controller to determine whether it should stop. Suppose the controller is required to produce a stop command within 20 ms after receiving a valid obstacle-detection event.

Situation Controller response Result A Correct STOP command in 8 ms Meets requirement B Correct STOP command in 15 ms Meets requirement C Correct STOP command in 35 ms Misses deadline D Incorrect MOVE command in 5 ms Functionally incorrect

Situation A and B both satisfy the functional and timing requirements. In Situation C produces the correct command but does not satisfy the timing requirement. Situation D responds quickly but produces the wrong command.

Note

The 20 ms requirement is an illustrative software deadline. A real robot's safe stopping requirements depend on its speed, sensing range, braking capability, mechanical characteristics, and other factors.

docs.title: Example 2: Robotic arm control
docs.text:
A robotic arm may use a controller that updates motor commands every 10 ms.

During each control cycle, the controller:

  1. Reads the measured joint position.
  2. Compares the measured position with the desired position.
  3. Calculates the next motor command.
  4. Sends the command to the motor driver.

If the controller is delayed, the motor command may be based on outdated information directly impacting accuracy of the arm' movement. Repeated delays or inconsistent update intervals can reduce control performance and, depending on the system, may affect stability.

There for reliable operation(s), the controller must execute according to its defined timing requirements.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Does real-time mean extremely fast?
docs.text:
A common misunderstanding is that a real-time system must always execute as quickly as possible. This is not necessarily true. The important requirement is that the system completes its operations within the specified timing constraints.

Consider two programs performing the same task.

Program A

  • Usually completes in 2 ms.
  • Occasionally takes 30 ms.

Program B

  • Consistently completes in 8 ms.
  • Never exceeds 10 ms under the tested conditions.

Suppose the task has a deadline of 15 ms.

Program A is usually faster, but it occasionally misses the deadline.

Program B is slower on average, but all its observed executions meet the deadline.

For this particular requirement, Program B demonstrates better timing behavior.

However, testing alone does not guarantee that Program B will always meet its deadline under every possible operating condition.

Remember

Real-time does not mean fastest. It means meeting timing requirements predictably.

A system that is very fast but frequently misses its deadlines may be unsuitable for a time-critical applications.

docs.title: 1.1.4 Real-time systems and ordinary computer programs
docs.text:
Consider a program that calculates the average of 1000 numbers. If the program takes 100 ms instead of 50 ms, the result is still mathematically correct. For many applications, this delay may be acceptable.

Now consider a robot controller that must update a motor command every 10 ms. If the controller occasionally takes 100 ms, the delay could significantly affect the robot's operation.

The main difference is that the robotic controller has explicit timing requirements that must be considered alongside its functional behaviour.

Ordinary application Real-time application Primarilyconcerned with producing the correct output/result Requires correct output within specified timing constraints Some delays maybe acceptable Delays may violate system requirements Execution time may be relatively flexible Timing constraints must be satisfied Example: generating a report Example: updating a motor controller

Note

The distinction isn't absolute! Ordinary applications can also have timing requirements, and not every robotic software function is strictly time-critical.

For example, generating a robot's daily activity report may not require strict real-time execution.

docs.title: 1.1.5 Where do we find real-time systems?
docs.text: Real-time computing is used in many applications where software must respond to events or complete operations within defined time limits.

docs.title: Robotics
docs.text:
• Motor/position control
  • Joint position control
  • Obstacle detection & avoidance
  • Motion stabilisation

docs.title: Automotive systems
docs.text:
• Engine control
  • ABS systems (Anti-lock braking systems)
  • ESC (Electronic stability control)

docs.title: Industrial automation
docs.text:
• Conveyor control
  • Industrial robot controllers
  • Automated production machinery

docs.title: Aerospace systems
docs.text:
• Flight control
  • Navigation & stabilisation
  • Aircraft control systems

The timing requirements of these applications can differ significantly.

Some tasks may need to execute every few milliseconds, while others may have deadlines measured in microseconds or seconds.

There is no single universal deadline that defines all real-time systems. What matters is whether the system meets the timing requirements of its particular application.

docs.title: 1.1.6 What happens when a deadline is missed?
docs.text:
A deadline is the latest permitted completion time for a task, measured relative to a defined reference event.

For example, if a task is released at time 0 ms and has a relative deadline of 20 ms, it must be completed by time 20 ms. If it completes at 12 ms, it meets the deadline. If it completes at 25 ms, it misses the deadline by 5 ms. A missed deadline does not necessarily mean that the system will immediately fail. Its consequences depend on what the task was and its application.

For example:

  • A delayed display update may only be inconvenient.
  • A delayed robot status message may be tolerable.
  • A delayed motor-control update may reduce performance.
  • A delayed safety-critical response may create a dangerous situation.

Later in this module, we will exam three important categories of real-time systems: hard, firm, and soft real-time systems, which describe different consequences of missing deadlines.

docs.title: 1.1.7 Real-time systems in this course
docs.text:
In this course, you will learn to design and evaluate software that performs operations according to timing requirements.

You will work with examples involving:

  • Periodic sensor readings
  • Concurrent software tasks
  • Task scheduling
  • Data sharing between tasks
  • Synchronisation mechanisms

  • Measuring execution time & timing variation

  • A normal PC (Windows, Linux or macOS) with C++17. The early labs use the PC to measure execution times, observe scheduling behaviour and investigate how a general-purpose operating system affects timing. No extra hardware is needed.

  • An ESP32 microcontroller board running FreeRTOS, programmed in C with ESP-IDF. Later labs use the board to run periodic and event-driven tasks that interact with real hardware, where timing must be predictable. The ESP32 has two processor cores, and you will learn to decide which core each task runs on (Section 1.5).

Important

A normal Windows or Linux computer does not automatically guarantee hard real-time execution. However, it provides a useful environment for learning how to measure execution times, observe scheduling behaviour, and investigate the effects of concurrent tasks. Comparing the timing you measure on the PC with the timing you measure on the microcontroller is one of the aims of this course.

docs.title: 1.2.1 How does a robot interact with its environment?
docs.text:
A robot interacts with the physical world through three fundamental operations:

  1. Sensing: Collecting information about the robot and its environment.
  2. Processing: Analysing information and determining what action to take.
  3. Actuation: Executing commands through motors or other actuators.

These operations form a continuous cycle.

docs.title: Example: Obstacle avoidance
docs.text:
Consider a mobile robot equipped with a distance sensor.

The robot performs the following operations:

  1. The sensor measures the distance to an obstacle.
  2. The controller reads the measurement.
  3. The controller determines whether the obstacle is too close.
  4. A command is sent to the motor driver.
  5. The motors respond to the command.

The cycle repeats while the robot is operating.

Key concept

A robot's response depends on the complete sensing–processing–actuation chain, not only on how quickly its controller executes.

For example, even if the controller performs its calculations very quickly, a slow sensor or delayed motor response can increase the total time needed to react.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Sources of delay in robotic systems
docs.text:
Every stage of the sensing–processing–actuation cycle requires some amount of time.

Common sources of delay include:

Source Description Sensor acquisition Time needed to obtain a measurement Communication Time needed to transfer sensor data or commands Scheduling Time spent waiting for the software task to execute Processing Time required to calculate a decision Actuator response Time needed for the actuator to begin or complete the requested action

These delays may occur at different stages of the system.

docs.title: Example: Robot obstacle response
docs.text:
Suppose a robot has the following response times:

Operation Time Sensor measurement 8 ms Sensor communication 2 ms Scheduling delay 3 ms Controller processing 4 ms Motor command communication 1 ms Total 18 ms

For this simplified example, the total delay is:

\[ T_{\text{response}} = 8 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 \] \[ \boxed{T_{\text{response}} = 18\ \text{ms}} \]

The calculated response time of 18 ms represents the time from the beginning of the sensor measurement until the motor command is delivered.

It does not include the additional time required for the motor and robot to physically slow down or stop.

Furthermore, the 18 ms value represents one assumed execution scenario. It does not guarantee that every execution will complete within 18 ms. Actual response times may vary because of scheduling, communication, and other system delays.

Note

Adding individual delays is appropriate when the operations occur sequentially without overlapping.

In more complex systems, some operations may overlap, and the overall response time must be determined from the actual execution sequence.

docs.title: Why is this important?
docs.text:
Suppose the software response deadline is 20 ms.

The example system completes its response in 18 ms and therefore meets this deadline.

However, it has only 2 ms of remaining time before the deadline.

If scheduling or communication takes longer than expected, the deadline may be missed.

This illustrates why engineers must consider the entire timing chain rather than only the processing time of the controller.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Different robotic functions have different timing requirements
docs.text:
Not all robotic tasks need to execute at the same speed.

Consider a mobile robot performing several operations simultaneously.

Robotic function Example timing requirement Reason Motor control Update every 10 ms Maintain controlled motion Distance sensing Measure every 50 ms Detect nearby obstacles Localization Update every 100 ms Estimate robot position Status reporting Update every 1 s Inform the user about robot state Data logging Save data every 5 s Store information for later analysis

These are illustrative values, not universal requirements.

The appropriate timing depends on the robot's speed, hardware, control algorithms, operating environment, and system requirements.

For example, a robot moving at high speed may need to detect and respond to obstacles more quickly than a slow-moving robot.

Similarly, a motor controller may need frequent updates, while a user-interface display can often tolerate longer delays.

Remember

A robotic system may contain several software tasks with different execution periods and deadlines.

A central challenge in real-time programming is ensuring that important tasks meet their timing requirements while sharing limited computing resources.

docs.title: Execution period versus deadline
docs.text:
Two important timing concepts are the period and the deadline.

  • Period: The time between consecutive intended activations of a recurring task.
  • Deadline: The latest time by which a task must complete, measured relative to its activation or another defined reference event.

For example, suppose a motor-control task is activated every 10 ms, but each execution must finish within 5 ms of its activation.

In this case:

  • Period: 10 ms
  • Relative deadline: 5 ms

The task is activated every 10 ms, but it has only 5 ms to complete each execution.

Note

A task's period and deadline are not necessarily equal. Their values depend on the system's requirements.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Periodic and Event-Driven Operations
docs.text:
Robotic software systems often perform multiple tasks, such as reading sensors, controlling motors, and processing communication messages. These tasks do not necessarily become ready to execute at the same time or for the same reason.

Two common ways of organising task activation are periodic activation and event-driven activation.

Before examining these approaches, it is important to distinguish between three concepts:

  • Task activation (release): The moment a new instance of a task becomes ready to execute.
  • Task execution: The time during which the processor actually runs the task.
  • Task completion: The moment the task finishes its work.

A task may become ready to execute but have to wait because the processor is busy with another task.

Key distinction

Activation does not necessarily mean immediate execution.

A task may be activated at a particular time, but its actual execution can begin later due to scheduling delays.

docs.title: Periodic operations
docs.text:
A periodic task is a software task that is activated at regular time intervals.

For example, a motor-control task may be activated every 10 ms to calculate and update the commands sent to the motors.

Its intended activation times could be:

\[ 0,\ 10,\ 20,\ 30,\ 40,\ 50,\ldots\ \text{ms} \]

The time between consecutive intended activations is called the period.

For this example:

\[ T = 10\ \text{ms} \]

The corresponding activation frequency is:

\[ f = \frac{1}{T} \]

Converting milliseconds to seconds:

\[ T = 0.010\ \text{s} \]

Therefore:

\[ \boxed{f = \frac{1}{0.010} = 100\ \text{Hz}} \]

This means that the motor-control task is intended to be activated 100 times per second.

However, the actual execution of each task instance may begin later because the processor could be busy executing another task.

docs.title: Example: Activation versus execution
docs.text:
Consider a motor-control task with a period of 10 ms.

Task instance Activation time Actual execution start Completion time 1 0 ms 1 ms 4 ms 2 10 ms 11.2 ms 14.6 ms 3 20 ms 20.7 ms 23.8 ms

Notice that:

  • The task is activated at regular 10 ms intervals.
  • The actual execution starts at slightly different times.
  • Each task instance takes some time to complete.

The difference between the activation time and the actual execution start time is the scheduling delay in this simplified example.

For instance, the second task instance is activated at 10 ms but starts executing at 11.2 ms.

Its scheduling delay is:

\[ T_{\text{delay}} = 11.2 - 10 \] \[ \boxed{T_{\text{delay}} = 1.2\ \text{ms}} \]

Note

A periodic task has regular intended activation times, but its actual execution start times may vary.

The task must also satisfy any specified deadline, which may be shorter than its period.

Typical periodic operations in robotics include:

  • Reading sensors at regular intervals.
  • Updating motor-control commands.
  • Estimating the robot's position.
  • Monitoring battery voltage.
  • Recording diagnostic information.

docs.title: Event-driven operations
docs.text:
An event-driven task is activated in response to a particular event rather than according to a fixed periodic schedule.

The event may occur at an unpredictable time.

Examples include:

  • A communication message arrives.
  • A limit switch changes state.
  • A hardware interrupt is generated.
  • A new sensor measurement becomes available.
  • A user presses a stop button.

For example, a robot may receive a wireless command at an unpredictable time.

When the message arrives, the system can activate a command-processing task.

However, just as with periodic tasks, activation does not necessarily mean immediate execution.

The task may have to wait until the processor becomes available or the scheduler selects it to run.

docs.title: Example: Wireless command processing
docs.text:
Suppose a robot receives a wireless command at 125 ms.

The following events occur:

Event Time Wireless message arrives 125 ms Command-processing task is activated 125 ms Task begins execution 127 ms Task completes processing 130 ms

In this example:

  • The task is activated when the message arrives.
  • The task begins executing 2 ms later.
  • The task completes processing 5 ms after the message arrives.

If the requirement is to complete processing within 10 ms after receiving the message, this execution meets the deadline.

Note

Event-driven does not automatically mean real-time.

An event-driven task must still satisfy its timing requirements if the application requires a bounded response.

Similarly, a periodic task is not necessarily hard real-time.

docs.title: Comparison: Periodic versus event-driven tasks
docs.text:
Feature Periodic task Event-driven task Activation At regular time intervals In response to an event Example Motor-control update Incoming communication message Timing Defined activation period Depends on event arrival Actual execution May be delayed by scheduling May be delayed by scheduling Typical requirement Complete each instance before its deadline Respond within a specified time after the event

Both approaches are widely used in robotics.

A robotic system may contain periodic and event-driven tasks operating simultaneously.

For example, a mobile robot might periodically update its motor-control commands while also responding to incoming wireless messages.

Task activation versus scheduling

Periodic and event-driven operations describe when software tasks become ready to execute.

These concepts are related to, but different from, clock-driven and event-driven scheduling, which describe how scheduling decisions are triggered or organised (Read More).

For example, a periodic motor-control task and an event-driven communication task can both be managed by the same operating-system scheduler.

We will explore scheduling mechanisms in Module 2.

docs.title: 1.2.5 How robot speed affects timing requirements
docs.text:
Timing requirements are often related to how quickly a robot moves.

Consider a mobile robot approaching an obstacle.

If the robot travels at a constant speed \(v\), the distance it travels during a time interval \(t\) is:

\[ d = vt \]

where:

  • \(d\) = distance traveled (m)
  • \(v\) = robot speed (m/s)
  • \(t\) = elapsed time (s)

docs.title: Example 1: Slow-moving robot
docs.text:
Suppose a robot moves at:

\[ v = 0.2\ \text{m/s} \]

Its software takes 100 ms to respond to an obstacle.

Convert the response time:

\[ t = 100\ \text{ms} = 0.1\ \text{s} \]

The robot travels:

\[ d = 0.2 \times 0.1 \] \[ \boxed{d = 0.02\ \text{m} = 2\ \text{cm}} \]

The robot moves 2 cm during the response delay.

docs.title: Example 2: Faster-moving robot
docs.text:
Now suppose the robot moves at:

\[ v = 1.0\ \text{m/s} \]

With the same response delay:

\[ d = 1.0 \times 0.1 \] \[ \boxed{d = 0.1\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{cm}} \]

The faster robot travels 10 cm during the same delay.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Robot speed Response delay Distance traveled 0.2 m/s 100 ms 2 cm 0.5 m/s 100 ms 5 cm 1.0 m/s 100 ms 10 cm 2.0 m/s 100 ms 20 cm

These calculations assume that the robot continues moving at a constant speed throughout the response delay.

Importantly, the calculated distance represents only the distance traveled before the robot begins responding to the stop command.

Even after the stop command is issued, the robot may continue moving while its motors slow down.

Therefore, the total stopping distance can be expressed as:

\[ \boxed{d_{\text{total}} = d_{\text{response}} + d_{\text{braking}}} \]

where:

\(d_{\text{response}}\) = distance traveled during the response delay, and

\(d_{\text{braking}}\) = additional distance traveled while slowing down.

For example, if a robot travels 10 cm during the response delay and another 15 cm while braking:

\[ d_{\text{total}} = 10 + 15 = 25\ \text{cm} \]

The robot therefore requires at least 25 cm to stop under these assumed conditions.

docs.title: What can we conclude?
docs.text:
As robot speed increases, a fixed response delay results in a greater distance traveled.

Therefore, faster-moving robots may require shorter response times, earlier obstacle detection, greater stopping distances, or a combination of these measures.

Timing requirements should be derived from the physical behavior and safety needs of the system.

docs.title: 1.2.6 Timing requirements and task priorities
docs.text:
A robot may execute several software tasks at the same time. For instance, motor control, sensor acquisition, obstacle detection, data logging, user-interface updates. These tasks compete for computing resources.

If a noncritical task occupies the processor while an important control task is waiting, the control task may be delayed.

Real-time systems therefore use scheduling mechanisms to determine which tasks execute and when.

Some tasks may be assigned higher scheduling priorities because their timing requirements are more demanding.

For example, a motor-control task may need to execute before a less time-critical data-logging task.

However, assigning a higher priority does not automatically guarantee that a task will meet its deadline. Execution times, resource sharing, scheduling delays, and other factors must also be considered.

We will explore task scheduling and priorities in detail in Module 2.

docs.title: 1.2.7 From application requirements to software requirements
docs.text:
A useful engineering approach is to begin with what the robot must accomplish and then identify the corresponding software timing requirements.

Consider the following simplified example.

Application requirement:

A mobile robot must detect nearby obstacles and respond before travelling an excessive distance.

Possible derived software requirements:

  1. The distance sensor shall provide a new measurement at least every 50 ms.
  2. The obstacle-processing task shall complete within 10 ms after receiving a valid measurement.
  3. The motor-command task shall deliver a STOP command within 10 ms after an obstacle condition is identified.

These requirements describe specific operations that can be implemented and tested.

Engineering principle

Good real-time requirements should be specific, measurable, and testable.

For example:

Vague requirement: "The robot should respond quickly."

Measurable requirement: "The controller shall produce a STOP command within 20 ms after receiving a valid obstacle-detection event."

The second statement provides a clear criterion for testing the software.

docs.title: Understanding the complete response time
docs.text:
The three requirements describe different stages of the robot's response.

Suppose an obstacle appears immediately after the sensor has taken a measurement.

If the sensor provides a new measurement every 50 ms, the robot may have to wait almost 50 ms before the obstacle is detected.

After receiving the new measurement:

  1. The obstacle-processing task may take up to 10 ms.
  2. The motor-command task may take another 10 ms.

Under these simplified assumptions, the total time could approach:

\[ T_{\text{response}} = 50 + 10 + 10 \] \[ \boxed{T_{\text{response}} = 70\ \text{ms}} \]

This example assumes that the specified delays cover the relevant stages and that no additional delays occur. A real system may also introduce sensor acquisition, communication, scheduling, and actuator delays.

Key distinction

Software response time may be measured from the moment a valid sensor measurement is received.

End-to-end response time considers the time from the occurrence of a physical event until the required system response is produced.

These are different timing requirements and must not be confused.

docs.title: How can we verify timing requirements?
docs.text:
Timing requirements should be measurable so that engineers can determine whether the system satisfies them.

One approach is to record timestamps at important stages of execution.

For example:

Event Timestamp Valid obstacle measurement received 100 ms Obstacle-processing task completed 107 ms STOP command delivered 115 ms

The processing time is:

\[ T_{\text{processing}} = 107 - 100 = 7\ \text{ms} \]

The motor-command delivery time after obstacle identification is:

\[ T_{\text{command}} = 115 - 107 = 8\ \text{ms} \]

Both operations satisfy their respective 10 ms deadlines in this execution.

The total software response time is:

\[ T_{\text{software}} = 115 - 100 = 15\ \text{ms} \]

This example demonstrates how timestamps can be used to evaluate timing requirements.

However, observing one successful execution does not prove that every future execution will meet its deadline. Engineers must consider timing variations and the system's operating conditions.

Later in this course, you will use C++ to measure execution times and investigate how scheduling affects task timing.

docs.title: 1.3.1 Why do we classify real-time systems?
docs.text:
In Chapter 1, we studied that a real-time system must produce correct results within specified timing constraints.

However, not every missed deadline has the same consequences.

Consider three situations:

  1. A safety-critical robot controller fails to respond within its required deadline.
  2. A robot's object-detection system produces a result too late for the current control decision.
  3. A robot's monitoring dashboard displays an update slightly later than expected.

All three situations involve timing delays, but their consequences are different.

In the first case, a missed deadline may violate a critical system requirement.

In the second case, the late result may no longer be useful.

In the third case, the information may still be useful despite the delay.

Real-time requirements are commonly classified into three categories:

  • Hard real-time
  • Firm real-time
  • Soft real-time

The classification depends primarily on the consequences of missing a deadline, not on how short the deadline is (Read more: Real-Time & Embedded Systems, Purdue University).

docs.title: 1.3.2 Hard real-time systems
docs.text:
A hard real-time requirement is one in which missing a deadline is considered a system failure. Every required deadline must be met for the system to satisfy its timing specification (Read more: Difference between hard & soft RTS - Geeksforgeeks).

In safety-critical applications, violating such a requirement may have serious consequences, such as injuries or more. For example, an air traffic control or surgical robotic arm.

docs.title: Example: Safety-critical robot stopping function
docs.text:
Consider an industrial robot operating near a hazardous area.

Suppose a safety-related controller has a validated requirement to generate a particular stop-related output within a specified time after receiving a safety input.

If the output is produced too late, the system violates its timing requirement.

Even if the output is logically correct, it does not satisfy the hard real-time specification.

Key concept

In hard real-time systems, missing a required deadline is unacceptable.

A correct result delivered too late does not satisfy the system's timing requirements.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Guaranteed response time: Deadlines must be met under the specified operating conditions.
  • Worst-case timing behaviour is important.
  • Timing requirements must be verified.
  • Missed deadlines represent violations of system correctness.

docs.title: Other examples
docs.text:
Depending on their design and requirements:

  • Safety-critical industrial robot control functions.
  • Aircraft flight-control functions.
  • Automotive braking-control functions.
  • Certain medical-device control functions.

Safety-critical systems

Meeting software deadlines is only one part of functional safety.

A real safety-related robotic system also requires appropriate risk assessment, hardware design, fault handling, verification and validation.

A hard real-time deadline alone does not guarantee that a robot is safe.

docs.title: 1.3.3 Firm real-time systems
docs.text:
A firm real-time requirement allows occasional deadline misses, but a result produced after its deadline is no longer useful (Read more: Difference between hard, firm, & soft) (Read more: Real-Time Embedded Systems, Linköping University).

Unlike hard real-time requirements, an occasional missed deadline does not necessarily mean the entire system has failed.

However, the late result may need to be discarded.

docs.title: Example: Robot camera processing
docs.text:
Imagine a mobile robot equipped with a camera, the camera produces images periodically, & the robot processes them to detect objects. Now let's suppose the robot receives a new image every 50 ms. And for a particular application, the controller requires an object-detection result before the next image-processing cycle.

If processing takes too long, the result may refer to an outdated scene.

For example:

Image Processing completion Deadline Result Frame 1 30 ms 50 ms Useful Frame 2 45 ms 50 ms Useful Frame 3 70 ms 50 ms Too late Frame 4 35 ms 50 ms Useful

In this example, the result for Frame 3 is considered too late and is discarded by the system. The system continues processing newer frames.

This illustrates a firm real-time requirement if occasional discarded frames are acceptable under the application's specification.

Key concept

In firm real-time systems, occasional deadline misses may be tolerated, but results produced after their deadlines have no value for the intended operation.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Occasional missed deadlines may be acceptable.
  • Late results are no longer useful.
  • The system may discard outdated results.
  • Repeated deadline misses may reduce system performance and/or eventually violate other requirements.

docs.title: Other examples
docs.text:
Depending on application requirements:

  • Processing camera frames for a robot's current perception cycle.
  • Updating an object-tracking result that becomes obsolete after a defined time.
  • Processing time-sensitive sensor data that must be replaced by newer measurements.

Note

A camera-processing task is not automatically firm real-time.

If its output is needed for a safety-critical function, its timing requirements may be hard real-time.

If late results remain useful, the requirement may instead be soft real-time.

docs.title: 1.3.4 Soft real-time systems
docs.text:
A soft real-time requirement is the one in which meeting deadlines is important, but occasional delays are acceptable (Read more).

A late result may still be useful, although its value/quality may decrease as the delay increases.

docs.title: Example: Robot monitoring dashboard
docs.text:
Consider a mobile robot sending its position, battery level, and operating status to a monitoring dashboard. Now if the dashboard is intended to update every 500 ms and an update, may occassionally, arrive after 650 ms.

The information is slightly delayed, but it may still be useful to the operator.

The robot can continue operating normally if this delay is permitted by the application requirements.

This is an example of a soft real-time requirement.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Deadlines are desirable but not necessarily strict.
  • Occasional delays may be acceptable.
  • Late results may retain some usefulness.
  • Excessive delays can reduce user experience/performance.

docs.title: Other examples
docs.text:
• Displaying robot status information.
  • Updating a noncritical visualisation.
  • Streaming video for general monitoring.
  • Presenting diagnostic information to an operator.

Key concept

In soft real-time systems, missed deadlines may reduce performance or quality without necessarily causing system failure.

docs.title: 1.3.5 Comparing hard, firm and soft real-time requirements
docs.text:
The main difference is the consequence of missing a deadline.

Characteristic Hard Firm Soft Every deadline MUST be met? Yes Not necessarily Not necessarily Are occasional misses acceptable? No Sometimes Sometimes Is a late result useful? Not acceptable for the specified deadline No May still be useful Consequence of a miss System requirement violated Result discarded or obsolete Quality or performance may decrease Robotics example Safety-critical control function Time-sensitive perception result Monitoring dashboard

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Hard and firm real-time requirements can both have a sharp deadline after which the result is no longer useful.

The difference is that:

  • Hard: A missed deadline violates a mandatory system requirement.
  • Firm: An occasional missed deadline is tolerated, but the late result is useless.

Soft real-time requirements differ because a result may still retain some value after its deadline.

docs.title: Visual comparison
docs.text: The following diagram summarises the typical consequences of missed deadlines.

docs.title: Visual comparison
docs.text:
The following flowchart shows how different real-time systems treat missed deadlines.

flowchart TD
    A["A task finishes after its deadline"]

    A --> B["Hard real-time"]
    A --> C["Firm real-time"]
    A --> D["Soft real-time"]

    B --> E["Deadline violation is unacceptable"]
    C --> F["Late result is no longer useful"]
    D --> G["Late result may still be useful"]
What does this mean?

  • Hard real-time: Missing a deadline violates a strict timing requirement. The system must be designed to prevent such misses.
  • Firm real-time: A result received after its deadline is no longer useful, although occasional deadline misses may be acceptable.
  • Soft real-time: A late result can still be useful, but the quality of the system's performance may decrease.

Remember

The main difference is not necessarily how fast the system operates, but how important it is to meet the deadline and what happens if the deadline is missed!

Remember

The classification is determined by the application's timing requirements and the consequences of missing them.

It is not determined simply by whether the deadline is 1 ms, 10 ms, or 1 second.

docs.title: 1.3.6 Can one robot contain all three types?
docs.text:
Yes.

A robotic system may contain several software functions with different timing requirements.

Consider an autonomous mobile robot operating in a warehouse.

Function Possible classification Reason Safety-critical stop-related control Hard Missing a required deadline violates a critical system requirement Object-detection result for the current processing cycle Firm An outdated result may be discarded Operator monitoring dashboard Soft Slightly delayed updates may remain useful

These classifications are illustrative and depend on the actual system design. The same function may have a different classification in another application. For example, object detection used for safety-critical collision prevention may have hard timing requirements, whereas object detection used only for collecting statistics may have soft timing requirements.

Therefore, engineers should classify individual timing requirements, rather than assuming that an entire robot belongs to one category.

docs.title: 1.3.7 What determines the correct classification?
docs.text:
When classifying a real-time requirement, consider three questions.

Question 1: What happens if the deadline is missed?

Does the missed deadline violate a mandatory system requirement, or can the system tolerate it?

Question 2: Is the result still useful after the deadline?

For example, an outdated sensor result may no longer be relevant, while a delayed status message may still be informative.

Question 3: How frequently can deadlines be missed?

An application may tolerate an occasional late result but fail to operate acceptably if delays occur repeatedly.

The answers help determine whether a requirement is hard, firm, or soft.

Note

In practice, some systems use more detailed timing models that specify how many deadlines may be missed within a particular sequence of executions.

These advanced models are beyond the scope of this introductory chapter.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Why do we need timing measurements?
docs.text:
Let's consider a mobile robot that must update its motor commands every 20 ms. The controller reads the robot's current speed, calculates a new motor command, and sends it to the motor driver. A successful calculation is not enough. The controller must also complete its work within the required time.

To evaluate this behaviour, we need to answer several questions:

  1. When should the task become ready to execute?
  2. When does it actually start?
  3. How long does it take to execute?
  4. When does it finish?
  5. Does it meet its deadline?
  6. Does its timing vary between executions?

Real-time engineers use specific timing concepts to answer these questions (View lecture notes).

Task versus task instance

A task is a software operation that may execute repeatedly.

Each individual execution is called a task instance, sometimes also called a job.

For example, a motor-control task released 100 times per second produces 100 task instances per second under its intended periodic schedule. Whether they execute and complete on time depends on the system.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Task release, start, and completion
docs.text: Before discussing execution time and deadlines, we need to distinguish between three important events.

docs.title: Release time
docs.text:
The release time is the instant at which a task instance becomes eligible for execution.

A task may be released by:

  • A periodic timer.
  • A hardware interrupt.
  • The arrival of a sensor measurement.
  • A communication event.

Release does not necessarily mean the processor starts executing the task immediately.

docs.title: Start time
docs.text:
The start time is when the processor actually begins executing the task instance.

A released task may have to wait because another task is executing or because it is waiting to be scheduled.

docs.title: Completion time
docs.text:
The completion time is when the task instance finishes its required operation.

Consider the following example.

A sensor-processing task is released at 0 ms, begins executing at 3 ms and completes at 9 ms.

In this example:

  • The task is released at 0 ms and becomes eligible to execute.
  • It starts at 3 ms, after waiting 3 ms.
  • It completes at 9 ms, after running continuously for 6 ms.
\[ \text{Waiting time} = 3 - 0 = 3\ \text{ms} \] \[ \text{Execution time} = 9 - 3 = 6\ \text{ms} \] \[ \text{Response time} = 9 - 0 = 9\ \text{ms} \]

Remember

Execution time measures CPU time consumed by the task instance.

Response time measures elapsed time from release to completion, including waiting and interruptions.

Note

In this simple example, the task executes continuously once it starts.

In a real operating system, a task may be interrupted, suspended, or blocked before completion.

Therefore, the time between start and completion is not always equal to the CPU execution time.

docs.title: 1.4.3 Execution time
docs.text:
Execution time is the amount of processor time required to execute a task instance.

For a task that executes continuously without interruption:

\[ C = t_{\text{finish}} - t_{\text{start}} \]

where:

  • \(C\) = execution time
  • \(t_{\text{start}}\) = task start time
  • \(t_{\text{finish}}\) = task completion time

This simple formula is valid when the task runs continuously during the measured interval.

docs.title: Example: Motor-control calculation
docs.text:
A motor-control task begins executing at 4 ms and finishes at 11 ms without interruption.

Its execution time is:

\[ C = 11 - 4 \] \[ \boxed{C = 7\ \text{ms}} \]

docs.title: What if a task is interrupted?
docs.text:
Suppose the task:

  1. Executes for 3 ms.
  2. Is interrupted by another task for 4 ms.
  3. Resumes and executes for another 2 ms.

Its CPU execution time is:

\[ C = 3 + 2 = 5\ \text{ms} \]

However, the elapsed time between its start and completion is:

\[ 3 + 4 + 2 = 9\ \text{ms} \]

This distinction matters because the task consumes only 5 ms of CPU time but takes 9 ms of elapsed time from its first start to completion.

The remaining 4 ms is spent in waiting state, while another task executes. Measuring only the time between start and completion therefore does not always reveal the actual CPU execution time.

docs.title: Worst-case execution time
docs.text:
A task may require different amounts of processing time depending on its inputs and execution path.

For example, an obstacle-detection algorithm may:

  • Process a small number of measurements in one execution.
  • Process a larger number of measurements in another execution.
  • Execute additional calculations when an obstacle is detected.

The worst-case execution time (WCET) is an upper bound on the processor execution time required by a task under specified conditions.

It is commonly represented by:

\[ C_{\text{WCET}} \]

For example, if a validated upper bound is 8 ms:

\[ C_{\text{WCET}} = 8\ \text{ms} \]

This means the task's CPU execution demand should not exceed 8 ms under the assumptions used to establish the bound.

Measured maximum versus WCET

The longest execution time observed during testing is not necessarily the true worst-case execution time.

Testing may not exercise every possible input, execution path, or operating conditions.

Establishing a dependable WCET bound can require more advanced analysis.

docs.title: 1.4.4 Task period and frequency
docs.text:
Many robotic functions execute periodically, e.g., reading an encoder every 5 ms, updating a motor controller every 10 ms, reading a distance sensor every 50 ms, or updating a monitoring display every 500 ms.

The period, represented by \(T\), is the intended time interval between consecutive releases of a periodic task.

docs.title: Example: Periodic motor control
docs.text:
Suppose a motor-control task is released every 20 ms.

Its release times are:

\[ 0,\ 20,\ 40,\ 60,\ 80,\ldots\ \text{ms} \]

Therefore:

\[ \boxed{T = 20\ \text{ms}} \]

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
Frequency tells us how many periodic cycles occur per second.

\[ \boxed{f = \frac{1}{T}} \]

where:

  • \(f\) = frequency in hertz (Hz)
  • \(T\) = period in seconds (s)

docs.title: Example 1
docs.text:
If a robot reads its wheel encoder every 10 ms.

Convert the period into seconds:

\[ T = 10\ \text{ms} = 0.010\ \text{s} \]

Calculate the frequency:

\[ f = \frac{1}{0.010} \] \[ \boxed{f = 100\ \text{Hz}} \]

The encoder-reading task is intended to be released 100 times per second. Whether each instance starts and completes on time depends on scheduling and execution delays.

docs.title: Example 2
docs.text:
Let's consider another example where a motor controller operates at 200 Hz. What is its period?

Now we can simply rearrange the frequency formula:

\[ T = \frac{1}{f} \]

Substitute:

\[ T = \frac{1}{200} = 0.005\ \text{s} \] \[ \boxed{T = 5\ \text{ms}} \]

docs.title: Common conversions
docs.text:
Period Frequency 1 ms 1000 Hz 5 ms 200 Hz 10 ms 100 Hz 20 ms 50 Hz 50 ms 20 Hz 100 ms 10 Hz 500 ms 2 Hz 1000 ms 1 Hz

Quick calculation

When the period is expressed in milliseconds:

\[ f = \frac{1000}{T_{\text{ms}}} \]

For example, a 25 ms period corresponds to:

\[ f = \frac{1000}{25} = 40\ \text{Hz} \]

docs.title: 1.4.5 Deadlines
docs.text:
A deadline is the latest permitted time by which a task instance must complete.

Deadlines are usually defined relative to a task's release time.

docs.title: Relative deadline
docs.text:
The relative deadline, \(D\), is the allowed interval between task release and required completion.

For example:

\[ D = 15\ \text{ms} \]

means the task must complete no later than 15 ms after its release.

docs.title: Absolute deadline
docs.text:
The absolute deadline, \(d\), is the actual point in time by which the task must finish.

It is calculated as:

\[ \boxed{d = r + D} \]

where:

  • \(r\) = release time
  • \(D\) = relative deadline
  • \(d\) = absolute deadline

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A task is released at:

\[ r = 40\ \text{ms} \]

Its relative deadline is:

\[ D = 12\ \text{ms} \]

The absolute deadline is:

\[ d = 40 + 12 \] \[ \boxed{d = 52\ \text{ms}} \]

The task must complete by 52 ms on the same timeline.

docs.title: Deadline versus period
docs.text:
A common mistake is assuming that the task's deadline must always equal its period. This is not true. Consider a task with:

\[ T = 20\ \text{ms} \]

and:

\[ D = 12\ \text{ms} \]

The task is released every 20 ms but must complete within 12 ms of each release.

Its first three releases and deadlines are:

Instance Release Absolute deadline 1 0 ms 12 ms 2 20 ms 32 ms 3 40 ms 52 ms

The task has 8 ms between each deadline and the next release.

docs.title: Example: Meeting a deadline
docs.text:
Suppose the first instance of this motor-control task is released at 0 ms. Its relative deadline is 12 ms, so its absolute deadline is 12 ms.

  • If it completes at 9 ms, it meets the deadline by 3 ms.
  • If it completes at 15 ms, it misses the deadline by 3 ms.
  • The next instance is still intended to be released at 20 ms.
Instance Release Deadline Example completion 1 0 ms 12 ms 9 ms (on time) 2 20 ms 32 ms 35 ms (late) 3 40 ms 52 ms 50 ms (on time)

Note

A period determines when the next instance is intended to be released. A deadline determines when the current instance must finish. They are not interchangeable.

In some systems, deadlines may also be longer than periods, allowing instances to overlap. That more advanced case is beyond the scope of this chapter.

Important

Period: How often a task is intended to be released.

Deadline: How soon each task instance must finish.

They describe different timing requirements.

docs.title: 1.4.6 Response time
docs.text:
The response time of a task instance is the elapsed time from its release until its completion.

It includes waiting, scheduling delays, execution, and any interruptions or blocking that occur before completion.

\[ \boxed{R = t_{\text{completion}} - r} \]

where:

  • \(R\) = response time
  • \(r\) = release time
  • \(t_{\text{completion}}\) = completion time

docs.title: Example: Sensor-processing task
docs.text:
Suppose:

  • Release time: 0 ms
  • Start time: 4 ms
  • Completion time: 13 ms

The response time is:

\[ R = 13 - 0 \] \[ \boxed{R = 13\ \text{ms}} \]

If the task executes continuously after starting, its execution time is:

\[ C = 13 - 4 = 9\ \text{ms} \]

The task therefore spends:

  • 4 ms waiting to start.
  • 9 ms executing.

Its total response time is 13 ms.

  1. At 0 ms — Release: The task becomes ready to execute, but the processor might be busy executing another task.
  2. At 4 ms — Start: The processor begins executing this task. It has waited 4 ms.
  3. At 13 ms — Completion: The task finishes executing. Since it started at 4 ms, its execution took \(13-4=9\) ms.

docs.title: Does the task meet its deadline?
docs.text:
Suppose its relative deadline is:

\[ D = 15\ \text{ms} \]

Since:

\[ R \leq D \]

the task meets its deadline.

docs.title: Deadline miss
docs.text:
If the task instead completes after 18 ms:

\[ R = 18\ \text{ms} \]

Since:

\[ R > D \]

the task misses its deadline.

The amount by which it misses the deadline is:

\[ M = R - D \] \[ M = 18 - 15 \] \[ \boxed{M = 3\ \text{ms}} \]

Note

The term response time may also refer to the complete response of a robotic system to an external event.

Always identify the start and end events of a measurement.

Task response time and end-to-end robot response time are not necessarily the same.

docs.title: 1.4.7 Deadline margin
docs.text:
Deadline margin is the difference between the completion time of a task instance and its deadline. It is also informally called the remaining time before the deadline.

For a completed task instance:

\[ \boxed{S = D - R} \]

where:

  • \(S\) = deadline margin, also referred to as slack
  • \(D\) = relative deadline
  • \(R\) = response time

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A task has:

\[ D = 20\ \text{ms} \]

and completes with:

\[ R = 16\ \text{ms} \]

Therefore:

\[ S = 20 - 16 \] \[ \boxed{S = 4\ \text{ms}} \]

The task finishes 4 ms before its deadline.

Interpretation:

Deadline margin (S) Meaning Positive Task finishes before its deadline Zero Task finishes exactly at its deadline Negative Task misses its deadline

For example:

\[ S = -3\ \text{ms} \]

means the task finishes 3 ms after its deadline.

Note

This calculation describes the observed deadline margin of a completed task instance.

In scheduling theory, slack or laxity may also describe the time remaining before a deadline after accounting for unfinished execution work.

docs.title: 1.4.8 Latency
docs.text: Latency is the delay between a defined event and a corresponding response. The exact meaning depends on what is being measured. In robotics, several types of latency are important.

docs.title: Sensor latency
docs.text: The time between a physical event/measurement and the availability of the corresponding sensor data.

docs.title: Scheduling latency
docs.text: The delay between a task becoming ready to execute and the operating system allowing it to begin or resume execution.

docs.title: Communication latency
docs.text: The time required for information to travel between components.

docs.title: End-to-end response latency
docs.text: The time between an external event and a specified system response.

docs.title: Example: Mobile robot obstacle response
docs.text:
Suppose a robot detects an obstacle. Its response chain contains:

Operation Time Sensor acquisition 6 ms Communication to controller 2 ms Scheduling delay 3 ms Controller processing 5 ms Motor-command transmission 2 ms

Assuming these stages occur sequentially:

\[ L_{\text{total}} = 6 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 2 \] \[ \boxed{L_{\text{total}} = 18\ \text{ms}} \]

The calculated 18 ms is the elapsed time from the beginning of the specified sensor acquisition operation until the motor command reaches the motor driver.

It is not necessarily the time from the instant an obstacle first appears: if sensing is periodic, the obstacle may appear just after a measurement, introducing additional waiting before the next measurement begins.

NOTE: Motor's response and the robot's physical braking time aren't included in the calculation above. Thus, the complete collision-avoidance response can be longer than 18 ms.

docs.title: Why does latency matter?
docs.text:
Suppose the robot travels at:

\[ v = 1.0\ \text{m/s} \]

During an 18 ms delay:

\[ t = 0.018\ \text{s} \]

Assuming constant speed:

\[ d = vt \] \[ d = 1.0 \times 0.018 \] \[ \boxed{d = 0.018\ \text{m} = 1.8\ \text{cm}} \]

The robot travels 1.8 cm before the command reaches the motor driver.

Actual stopping distance will be greater because the robot still needs to decelerate.

Warning

Latency calculations must use clearly defined start and end events.

For example, measuring from the start of sensor acquisition is different from measuring from the instant an obstacle first enters the sensor's detection range.

docs.title: 1.4.9 Jitter
docs.text:
Even when a task is intended to execute at regular intervals, its actual timing may vary. This variation is called jitter.

In real-time systems, jitter can refer to variations in:

  • Task activation/release times
  • Task start times
  • Completion times
  • Execution intervals
  • Response latency

It is important to specify which type is being measured.

docs.title: Example: Variation in motor-control task start times
docs.text:
A motor-control task has a nominal period of 10 ms. For this example, let's suppose its ideal execution starts coincide with the intended releases.

Its ideal start times are:

\[ 0,\ 10,\ 20,\ 30,\ 40\ \text{ms} \]

However, the measured start times are:

\[ 0,\ 11,\ 20,\ 32,\ 41\ \text{ms} \]

The actual intervals between consecutive starts are:

\[ 11,\ 9,\ 12,\ 9\ \text{ms} \]

These intervals are not identical.

docs.title: Start-interval deviation
docs.text:
Here we measure variation in the intervals between consecutive execution starts. We define the signed start-interval deviation as:

\[ \boxed{J_i = T_{\text{actual},i} - T_{\text{nominal}}} \]

where:

  • \(J_i\) = signed deviation for interval \(i\)
  • \(T_{\text{actual},i}\) = measured interval
  • \(T_{\text{nominal}}\) = intended period

For a nominal period of 10 ms:

Actual interval Signed deviation 11 ms +1 ms 9 ms -1 ms 12 ms +2 ms 9 ms -1 ms

A positive value means the interval is longer than intended.

A negative value means the interval is shorter than intended.

docs.title: Maximum absolute start-interval deviation
docs.text:
A simple summary measure is:

\[ J_{\max} = \max_i |J_i| \]

For the example:

\[ J_{\max} = \max(1,1,2,1) \] \[ \boxed{J_{\max} = 2\ \text{ms}} \]

The largest observed deviation of the measured start-to-start intervals from the nominal period is 2 ms. This is not a measurement of release jitter.

Jitter terminology

Different technical sources use different jitter metrics.

For example, engineers may measure maximum absolute period deviation, peak-to-peak variation, release jitter, or start-time jitter.

Therefore, always state the metric used.

docs.title: Why does jitter matter in robotics?
docs.text:
Consider a controller that expects fresh sensor information every 10 ms. If actual updates occur at irregular intervals, the controller may receive measurements earlier or later than expected.

This can affect:

  • Control-loop consistency,
  • Sensor-data timing,
  • Motion estimation,
  • Coordination between software tasks

The effect depends on the controller design and the magnitude of the variation.

docs.title: 1.4.10 Why periodic timing can drift?
docs.text:
Consider a simple program that repeatedly performs an operation and then waits for 10 ms.

REPEAT:
    Perform task
    Wait 10 ms

Suppose the task takes 3 ms to execute. Ignoring other delays, each cycle takes:

\[ T_{\text{cycle}} = 3 + 10 \] \[ \boxed{T_{\text{cycle}} = 13\ \text{ms}} \]

The program therefore starts the task approximately every 13 ms, not every 10 ms. If execution time varies, the start-to-start interval varies too.

docs.title: Why does this cause timing drift?
docs.text:
Suppose a motor controller is intended to update its commands every 10 ms.

Its ideal release times are:

\[ 0,\ 10,\ 20,\ 30,\ 40,\ldots\ \text{ms} \]

With 3 ms of work followed by a 10 ms wait, its approximate actual start times instead become:

\[ 0,\ 13,\ 26,\ 39,\ 52,\ldots\ \text{ms} \]

The difference from the intended schedule grows over successive cycles. This is accumulated timing drift.

docs.title: A better approach: Fixed periodic timing
docs.text:
Instead of waiting for a fixed duration after each execution, the program can follow fixed intended release times:

SET period = 10 ms
SET next_release = current_time

REPEAT:
    WAIT until next_release
    Perform task
    next_release = next_release + period

The intended release times remain:

\[ 0,\ 10,\ 20,\ 30,\ 40,\ldots\ \text{ms} \]

If each execution takes 3 ms, starts exactly on time, and runs without interruption:

Intended release Execution interval Next intended release 0 ms 0–3 ms 10 ms 10 ms 10–13 ms 20 ms 20 ms 20–23 ms 30 ms 30 ms 30–33 ms 40 ms

The execution time is no longer added to the intended period.

Note

These are idealised times. In a real operating system, actual task execution may start late because of scheduling delays.

docs.title: What happens if the task takes too long?
docs.text:
Suppose a task has a period of 10 ms but takes 12 ms to complete. The next intended release occurs before the previous instance has finished: the task has overrun its period.

A fixed periodic schedule does not solve an overrun automatically. The software needs a defined policy for missed releases or unfinished work, such as reporting a timing violation or skipping an outdated update when appropriate.

docs.title: Real-world implementation
docs.text:
FreeRTOS provides vTaskDelayUntil() and xTaskDelayUntil() for periodic timing. These functions calculate wake-up times relative to a previous wake-up reference rather than adding a fixed wait after each execution (View official FreeRTOS documentation).

We will explore this approach in later programming exercises.

Key concept

A fixed periodic schedule helps prevent accumulated timing drift.

It does not guarantee that every task starts exactly on time or meets its deadline. Actual timing still depends on execution demand, scheduling and system workload.

docs.title: 1.4.11 Detailed example: Robot motor controller
docs.text:
A mobile robot has a periodic motor-control task.

The task has the following requirements:

  • Period: 20 ms
  • Relative deadline: 15 ms

For one execution, the measured times are:

  • Release: 40 ms
  • Start: 44 ms
  • Completion: 53 ms

Calculate:

  1. Task frequency.
  2. Absolute deadline.
  3. Waiting time before execution.
  4. Execution time, assuming uninterrupted execution.
  5. Response time.
  6. Deadline margin.
  7. Whether the deadline is met.

Note

Before scorlling down for the solution, try to calculate yourself on a piece of paper.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Frequency \[ T = 20\ \text{ms} = 0.020\ \text{s} \] \[ f = \frac{1}{0.020} \] \[ \boxed{f = 50\ \text{Hz}} \] 2. Absolute deadline \[ d = r + D \] \[ d = 40 + 15 \] \[ \boxed{d = 55\ \text{ms}} \] 3. Waiting time \[ W = 44 - 40 \] \[ \boxed{W = 4\ \text{ms}} \] 4. Execution time \[ C = 53 - 44 \] \[ \boxed{C = 9\ \text{ms}} \] 5. Response time \[ R = 53 - 40 \] \[ \boxed{R = 13\ \text{ms}} \] 6. Deadline margin \[ S = D - R \] \[ S = 15 - 13 \] \[ \boxed{S = 2\ \text{ms}} \] 7. Deadline evaluation

The response time is 13 ms, which is less than the 15 ms deadline.

Therefore, the task meets its deadline with a 2 ms margin.
