docs.title: 1.5 General-purpose Operating Systems versus Real-time Operating Systems
1.5.1 Why do robots need operating systems?
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, we learned that robotic software must often perform several operations within specified timing constraints.

Consider an autonomous mobile robot, it may need to read distance sensors, calculate motor commands, monitor battery voltage, communicate with another computer, or record diagnostic information.

These operations may need to happen repeatedly, and some may need to happen concurrently.

  • But who decides which operation runs first?

  • Who determines when a waiting task can execute?

  • Who manages access to the processor and other hardware resources?

These responsibilities are commonly handled by an operating system (OS).

An operating system is software that manages computing resources and provides services to applications. Typical responsibilities include: Scheduling software tasks, Managing memory, Handling hardware interrupts, Providing communication mechanisms, Managing input and output, Coordinating access to shared resources.

docs.title: Let's take an example of Mobile robot controller
docs.text:
A robot controller may contain three tasks:

Task Function Example period Sensor task Read distance measurements 50 ms Control task Calculate motor commands 20 ms Logging task Record system information 500 ms

All three tasks may need processor time.

On a single-core processor, only one task can execute on that core at a particular instant.

The operating system's scheduler helps decide which ready task executes (Read more: Process Scheduling in OS - Geekforgeeks).

Note

Not every robot requires an operating system.

A simple microcontroller can execute a single program directly without a conventional OS. This is commonly called bare-metal programming.

An RTOS becomes useful when the application needs structured task scheduling, concurrency, and other operating-system services.

docs.title: 1.5.2 General-purpose operating systems
docs.text:
A general-purpose operating system (GPOS) is designed to support a wide variety of applications and workloads. E.g., Microsoft Windows, Standard desktop Linux distributions, macOS.

These systems are designed to provide capabilities such as:

  • running multiple applications,
  • supporting graphical user interfaces,
  • managing files and storage,
  • providing networking services,
  • sharing computing resources,
  • maintaining good overall performance and responsiveness.

docs.title: Example: Windows laptop
docs.text:
Imagine running the following applications simultaneously: VS Code, a web browser, a music player,a C++ robotics simulator. The operating system manages these applications and shares the available computing resources between them. This works well for ordinary computing.

However, suppose your robotics simulation contains a control task that should execute every 10 ms. Other system activities may affect when the task actually executes. For instance, background applications may consume processor time, device drivers may perform some tasks, the OS may schedule another task, memory management may introduce delays.

As a result, the task may occasionally start later than intended.

Key concept

A GPOS usually aims to provide good overall performance & responsiveness.

It doesn't automatically guarantee that an ordinary application will meet every real-time deadline.

This does not mean that Windows or standard Linux cannot execute time-sensitive programs. They can, and they are useful for learning, simulation, development, and many robotics applications.

The important distinction is between observed timing performance and a guaranteed timing bound.

docs.title: 1.5.3 Real-time operating systems
docs.text:
A real-time operating system (RTOS) is designed to support applications with explicit timing requirements.

An RTOS typically provides mechanisms for:

  • Task scheduling,
  • Task priorities,
  • Pre-emption,
  • Timers and periodic execution,
  • Interrupt handling,
  • Task synchronisation,
  • Inter-task communication

The objective is to make timing behaviour sufficiently predictable for the application's requirements.

docs.title: Example: Embedded robot controller
docs.text:
Let's consider a microcontroller controlling a mobile robot. The controller executes a high-priority motor-control task, a medium-priority sensor task, & a lower-priority logging task.

Now let's suppose the logging task is currently running when the motor-control task becomes ready. With a suitable pre-emptive scheduling configuration, the RTOS can interrupt the logging task and allow the higher-priority motor-control task to execute.

This reduces the time the control task spends waiting for lower-priority work.

Important

An RTOS does not automatically guarantee that every deadline will be met.

Meeting deadlines also depends on execution times, priorities, resource sharing, interrupt behaviour, hardware, and the overall system design.

A widely used example is FreeRTOS, a real-time operating-system kernel commonly used in embedded systems.

Its default single-core scheduling policy uses fixed priorities and pre-emption (Read more: FreeRTOS Scheduling - FreeRTOS Documentation).

docs.title: 1.5.4 What is task scheduling?
docs.text:
Task scheduling is the process of deciding which task should execute on the processor.

Consider a single-core processor with three ready tasks:

Task Function Priority A Motor control High B Sensor processing Medium C Data logging Low

If all three tasks are ready and the scheduler uses fixed-priority pre-emptive scheduling, Task A is selected first.

When Task A finishes or blocks, the scheduler can select Task B.

Task C runs when no higher-priority task is ready.

docs.title: Figure 1.5.1: Simplified task scheduler
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Tasks become ready"] --> B["Operating-system scheduler"]
    B --> C{"Which ready task has the highest priority?"}
    C --> D["Select task"]
    D --> E["Execute on CPU"]
    E --> F{"Task completes, blocks or is pre-empted?"}
    F --> G["Update task states"]
    G --> B

This is a simplified representation of priority-based scheduling.

Actual operating systems may use different scheduling policies and additional rules.

docs.title: Why is scheduling important?
docs.text:
Suppose the motor-control task must complete within 10 ms.

If it waits too long before executing, it may miss its deadline even if its calculations require only 2 ms of processor time.

From previous chapter, we know that

\[ R = t_{\text{completion}} - r \]

where:

  • \(R\) = task response time.
  • \(r\) = release time.
  • \(t_{\text{completion}}\) = completion time.

Scheduling delays contribute to the response time.

Therefore, scheduling behaviour is an important part of real-time system design.

docs.title: 1.5.5 Pre-emptive versus non-pre-emptive (cooperative) scheduling
docs.text:
Operating systems use different scheduling approaches to determine when tasks can execute and whether a running task can be interrupted.

Two important approaches are:

  1. Pre-emptive scheduling
  2. Non-pre-emptive scheduling, which includes cooperative scheduling

The fundamental difference is whether the scheduler can forcibly take the processor away from a running task to execute another task.

docs.title: Pre-emptive scheduling
docs.text:
In pre-emptive scheduling, the operating system can interrupt a running task and allow another task to execute, according to its scheduling policy. For example, in a fixed-priority pre-emptive system, a high-priority motor-control task may become ready while a lower-priority logging task is running. The scheduler can pre-empt (temporarily suspend) the logging task and allow the higher-priority motor-control task to execute. Once the motor-control task finishes or blocks, the logging task may resume.

This approach is particularly useful in robotics because time-critical tasks can receive processor time without waiting for lower-priority tasks to finish.

docs.title: Pre-emptive scheduling example:
docs.text:
Let's consider a robot with two tasks:

  • Task L: Low-priority data logging.
  • Task H: High-priority motor control.

Now let's assume the following:

  • Task L starts executing at 0 ms and requires 10 ms of CPU time.
  • Task H becomes ready (is released) at 3 ms.
  • Task H requires 2 ms of uninterrupted execution.
  • The processor has a single core.
  • Scheduling and context-switching overheads are ignored.

The execution sequence is:

The response time of Task H is calculated as:

\[ R_H = t_{\text{completion}} - r \]

where:

  • \(R_H\) = response time of Task H
  • \(r\) = release time
  • \(t_{\text{completion}}\) = completion time

Substituting the values:

\[ R_H = 5 - 3 \] \[ \boxed{R_H = 2\ \text{ms}} \]

Task H responds quickly because it does not have to wait for the lower-priority task to finish.

Note

Pre-emption does not mean that a higher-priority task will always execute instantaneously.

In a real system, context-switching overhead, interrupt handling, and other factors may introduce additional delays.

docs.title: Non-pre-emptive scheduling
docs.text:
In non-pre-emptive scheduling, the scheduler does not forcibly interrupt a running task simply because another task becomes ready.

Once a task begins executing, it retains the processor until it:

  • completes its execution,
  • blocks while waiting for an event or resource,
  • or voluntarily yields control, if supported by the scheduling system.

Consequently, even a high-priority task may have to wait while a lower-priority task is executing.

docs.title: Cooperative scheduling
docs.text:
Cooperative scheduling is a form of non-pre-emptive scheduling.

In cooperative scheduling, tasks voluntarily cooperate by yielding control or blocking so that other ready tasks can execute.

For example, a task may call an operating-system function to yield the processor after completing part of its work.

Unlike pre-emptive scheduling, the operating system does not forcibly interrupt the task merely because a higher-priority task becomes ready.

Key distinction

Non-pre-emptive scheduling is the broader category in which a running task is not forcibly displaced by the scheduler.

Cooperative scheduling is a form of non-pre-emptive scheduling that relies on tasks voluntarily yielding or blocking to allow other tasks to run.

The terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but they are not always identical.

docs.title: Non-pre-emptive scheduling example:
docs.text:
Consider the same two tasks:

  • Task L: Low-priority data logging.
  • Task H: High-priority motor control.

Let's assume the following:

  • Task L starts executing at 0 ms.
  • Task L requires 10 ms of uninterrupted execution.
  • Task H becomes ready at 3 ms.
  • Task H requires 2 ms of execution.
  • Task L does not yield or block before completing.
  • Scheduling overhead is ignored.

The execution sequence is:

docs.title: Figure 1.5.1: Non-pre-emptive scheduling timeline
docs.text:
Step-by-step explanation:

  1. At 0 ms, Task L begins executing.
  2. At 3 ms, Task H becomes ready.
  3. Task H cannot pre-empt Task L.
  4. Task L continues executing until 10 ms.
  5. At 10 ms, Task L finishes and releases the processor.
  6. Task H begins executing at 10 ms and completes at 12 ms.

The response time of Task H is:

\[ R_H = t_{\text{completion}} - r \] \[ R_H = 12 - 3 \] \[ \boxed{R_H = 9\ \text{ms}} \]

Although Task H requires only 2 ms of CPU execution time, its response time is 9 ms because it must wait for Task L.

The waiting time is:

\[ W_H = 10 - 3 \] \[ \boxed{W_H = 7\ \text{ms}} \]

Therefore:

\[ R_H = W_H + C_H \] \[ R_H = 7 + 2 = 9\ \text{ms} \]

This relationship holds for this example because Task H executes continuously after it starts.

What if Task L yields earlier?

Suppose Task L voluntarily yields at 4 ms instead of continuing until 10 ms.

If the scheduler selects Task H immediately, Task H can execute from 4 ms to 6 ms.

Its response time becomes:

\[ R_H = 6 - 3 = 3\ \text{ms} \]

This demonstrates how cooperative scheduling can improve responsiveness when tasks yield frequently enough.

docs.title: Comparison: Pre-emptive versus non-pre-emptive scheduling
docs.text: Feature Pre-emptive scheduling Non-pre-emptive scheduling Can a running task be forcibly interrupted by the scheduler? Yes, according to scheduling rules No, not merely to schedule another ready task Can a higher-priority task immediately replace a lower-priority task? Usually, if pre-emption is permitted No; it must wait for the running task to relinquish the processor Response to time-critical tasks Often faster Depends on how long other tasks continue executing Programming complexity Requires careful handling of concurrent access to shared data Can simplify some concurrency concerns Risk of long waiting times Still possible because of blocking and other delays Higher when tasks execute for long periods without yielding Typical use Many RTOS configurations and GPOS Cooperative task loops and some embedded scheduling configurations

docs.title: Comparing the examples
docs.text:
Both examples use the same tasks and execution requirements.

Measurement Pre-emptive Non-pre-emptive Task H release time 3 ms 3 ms Task H start time 3 ms 10 ms Task H execution time 2 ms 2 ms Task H completion time 5 ms 12 ms Task H waiting time 0 ms 7 ms Task H response time 2 ms 9 ms

The high-priority motor-control task completes 7 ms earlier in the pre-emptive example.

Suppose Task H has a relative deadline of:

\[ D_H = 5\ \text{ms} \]

For pre-emptive scheduling:

\[ R_H = 2\ \text{ms} \leq 5\ \text{ms} \]

The task meets its deadline.

For non-pre-emptive scheduling:

\[ R_H = 9\ \text{ms} > 5\ \text{ms} \]

The task misses its deadline by 4 ms.

This illustrates why the choice of scheduling approach can significantly affect the timing behaviour of robotic systems.

Important considerations

Pre-emptive scheduling improves flexibility and can reduce the response time of high-priority tasks.

However, it also introduces additional challenges when tasks share data or resources.

Non-pre-emptive scheduling can simplify certain aspects of programming, but long-running tasks may delay time-critical operations.

Neither approach automatically guarantees that all deadlines will be met.

**task concurrency and scheduling will be studied in more detail in the next Module.

docs.title: 1.5.6 Task states in an RTOS
docs.text:
An RTOS typically manages tasks using several states.

Three important states are:

Running: The task is currently executing on a processor.

Ready: The task can execute but is waiting to be selected by the scheduler.

Blocked: The task is waiting for an event, such as a timer, message, or synchronisation condition.

A task may also be suspended, depending on the OS.

flowchart TD
    A["Ready"] -->|"Selected by scheduler"| B["Running"]
    B -->|"Pre-empted or yields"| A
    B -->|"Waits for timer or event"| C["Blocked"]
    C -->|"Timer expires or event occurs"| A

docs.title: Figure 1.5.2: Simplified task-state transitions
docs.text:
For example, suppose a sensor task is intended to execute every 50 ms (periodically).

  1. The task waits for its next scheduled release.
  2. When the timer condition is satisfied, it becomes ready.
  3. The scheduler selects the task.
  4. The task reads the sensor.
  5. The task waits for its next release.

The cycle repeats.

Tip

A blocked task does not continuously consume CPU time while waiting.

This allows the processor to execute other ready tasks or enter an idle state.

docs.title: 1.5.7 Polling versus interrupts
docs.text:
Robotic controllers need to respond to hardware events.

Two common approaches are polling and interrupts (Read more: Pooling vs Interrupts).

docs.title: Polling
docs.text:
In polling, software repeatedly checks whether an event has occurred.

For example:

REPEAT:
    Check whether a button is pressed

    IF button is pressed:
        Process button event

This approach is straightforward. However, if the programme checks continuously, it may consume processor time unnecessarily. If it checks only occasionally, an event may not be detected immediately.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
An interrupt is a mechanism that allows hardware or software to request the processor's attention.

For example, a microcontroller may receive an interrupt when:

  • A timer reaches a specified value.
  • A digital input changes state.
  • A communication peripheral receives data.
  • A sensor indicates that a measurement is ready.

The processor may temporarily interrupt normal execution to handle the event.

A short function called an interrupt service routine (ISR) handles the immediate interrupt-related work.

E.g., a robot uses a wheel encoder that generates pulses as the wheel rotates.

Polling approach:

The programme repeatedly reads the encoder input to check whether a pulse has occurred.

Interrupt approach:

An appropriate hardware event can trigger an interrupt when an encoder signal changes.

The interrupt handler can record the event or notify a processing task.

flowchart TD
    A["Hardware event"] --> B["Interrupt request"]
    B --> C["Interrupt service routine"]
    C --> D["Record event or notify task"]
    D --> E["Task becomes ready"]
    E --> F["Scheduler selects task"]
    F --> G["Process event"]

docs.title: Figure 1.5.3: Interrupt-driven processing
docs.text:
Important

Interrupts do not automatically guarantee immediate application-level processing.

Interrupt latency, interrupt masking, scheduling, and other system activities can introduce delays.

Interrupt handlers should generally perform only the necessary immediate work and leave longer processing to an appropriate task.

docs.title: 1.5.8 Why can timing become unpredictable?
docs.text: Even with an RTOS, software execution may experience timing variation. Some of the common causes are:

docs.title: 1. Higher-priority tasks
docs.text: A lower-priority task may be interrupted when a higher-priority task becomes ready.

docs.title: 2. Interrupt handling
docs.text:
Hardware interrupts require processor time.

Depending on the system, they may delay normal task execution.

docs.title: 3. Shared resources
docs.text:
Two tasks may need access to the same data or hardware resource.

One task may have to wait until another releases the resource.

docs.title: 4. Memory management
docs.text: Operations such as dynamic memory allocation and page faults may introduce variable delays.

docs.title: 5. Communication
docs.text: Waiting for data from a peripheral or another computer may introduce delays.

docs.title: 6. Hardware and system behaviour
docs.text:
Cache effects, memory access, firmware, and other hardware activities can influence timing.

For instacne, if a motor-control task usually takes 3 ms to complete. However, it occassionally takes 9 ms because it is delayed by other system activity. If its deadline is 5 ms, those delayed executions violate the requirement.

Simply using a faster processor does not necessarily eliminate every source of unpredictable delay.

For demanding real-time applications, engineers must consider the entire software and hardware execution path.

The ROS 2 real-time programming guidance specifically discusses avoiding unbounded blocking, page faults, and unpredictable memory operations in time-critical execution paths (Read more: ROS 2 Design Documentation).

docs.title: 1.5.9 Comparing Windows, Linux, & FreeRTOS
docs.text: Different operating systems are suitable for different robotics applications.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows is a general-purpose operating system. It is widely used for:

  • Robotics software development.
  • Simulation.
  • Data analysis.
  • Graphical applications.
  • Programming and testing.

Standard Windows applications don't automatically receive hard real-time scheduling guarantees.

docs.title: Standard Linux
docs.text:
Linux is widely used in robotics because it supports:

  • Programming and software development.
  • Networking and communication.
  • Robot middleware.
  • Hardware interfaces.
  • Robotics frameworks such as ROS 2.

Standard Linux can run time-sensitive applications, but its default scheduling configuration does not automatically guarantee strict real-time deadlines.

docs.title: Linux with PREEMPT_RT
docs.text:
Linux can also be configured with real-time pre-emption support.

The PREEMPT_RT approach reduces scheduling latency by making more kernel execution paths pre-emptible.

This makes Linux more suitable for applications requiring predictable scheduling behaviour.

However, a real-time Linux kernel does not guarantee that an incorrectly designed application will meet its deadlines.

The Linux kernel documentation explains the changes introduced by PREEMPT_RT, including threaded interrupts and real-time locking mechanisms (Read more: Real-time Pre-emption — Theory of Operation).

docs.title: FreeRTOS
docs.text:
FreeRTOS is a real-time operating-system kernel commonly used in microcontroller-based embedded systems. It provides mechanisms such as:

  • Tasks.
  • Priorities.
  • Scheduling.
  • Timers.
  • Queues.
  • Semaphores.
  • Mutexes.

It is suitable for many small embedded robotics controllers.

For example, an ESP32 microcontroller can use FreeRTOS to organise sensor acquisition, motor control, and communication tasks.

docs.title: Comparison table
docs.text:
Characteristic Windows Standard Linux Linux with PREEMPT_RT FreeRTOS Main focus General computing General computing and embedded applications Linux with improved real-time behaviour Embedded real-time applications Typical hardware PCs PCs and embedded computers PCs and embedded computers Microcontrollers Multitasking Yes Yes Yes Yes Task priorities Yes Yes Yes Yes Real-time scheduling mechanisms Available, but standard applications lack hard real-time guarantees Available with suitable policies and configuration Enhanced real-time pre-emption Designed for real-time task scheduling Typical robotics use Development and simulation Robot computers and ROS 2 Time-sensitive robot computing Embedded controllers

Important

An RTOS is not necessarily faster than a GPOS.

Its advantage is the ability to support more predictable timing through appropriate scheduling and system design.

docs.title: 1.5.10 Example: A robot with two computing systems
docs.text:
While working on projects, we have already come across situations where a robot may contain both a general-purpose computer and a microcontroller.

Consider a mobile robot equipped with:

  • Raspberry Pi running Linux,
  • an ESP32 microcontroller running FreeRTOS,
  • a distance sensor,
  • wheel encoders,
  • motor drivers.

The Raspberry Pi might perform: camera processing, mapping, path planning, user communication.

The ESP32 might perform: wheel-speed control, encoder acquisition, motor-driver control, time-critical local monitoring.

flowchart TD
    A["Raspberry Pi<br/>Linux"]
    B["ESP32<br/>FreeRTOS"]
    C["Camera"]
    D["User interface (UI)"]
    E["Wheel encoders"]
    F["Motor drivers"]
    G["Motors"]

    C --> A
    D <--> A
    A <-->|"Commands and status"| B
    E --> B
    B --> F
    F --> G

docs.title: Figure 1.5.4: Computing architecture may look like
docs.text: This division allows the embedded controller to manage local timing requirements while the larger computer handles more computationally demanding operations.

docs.title: 1.5.11 Choosing an operating-system approach
docs.text:
When selecting an operating system, engineers should consider:

  1. The required timing behaviour
  2. The processor and hardware platform
  3. The number and types of software tasks
  4. The consequences of missed deadlines
  5. Memory and processing constraints
  6. Communication requirements
  7. Development and maintenance needs

This is a simplified decision guide. The operating system is only one component of the overall solution.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Why do robots need to perform multiple activities?
docs.text:
Consider an autonomous mobile robot moving through a laboratory.

While moving, the robot must perform several activities:

  1. Read its distance sensor.
  2. Calculate the required motor speeds.
  3. Send commands to the motor drivers.
  4. Monitor the battery voltage.
  5. Record diagnostic information.

Some activities need frequent execution, while others can occur less often.

For example:

Activity Example period Frequency Motor control 10 ms 100 Hz Distance measurement 50 ms 20 Hz Battery monitoring 500 ms 2 Hz Data logging 1000 ms 1 Hz

The motor controller may need frequent updates to maintain stable motion, whereas battery monitoring may not require such frequent execution. The challenge is to organise these activities so that each receives sufficient processor time and satisfies its timing requirements.

A robot does not necessarily need multiple processor cores to handle these activities. Even a single-core processor can manage multiple tasks by switching between them.

This leads us to the concepts of sequential execution, concurrency, and parallelism.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Sequential programming
docs.text:
In sequential programming, instructions execute in a defined order within a single flow of execution.

One operation must finish before the next operation begins.

For example:

START
  |
  v
Read distance sensor
  |
  v
Calculate motor command
  |
  v
Send motor command
  |
  v
Record diagnostic data
  |
  v
END

This is a sequential program.

The program completes each operation before proceeding to the next.

docs.title: C++ example 1: Sequential robot operations
docs.text:
Consider the following C++ program:

#include <iostream>

void readSensor()
{
    std::cout << "Reading distance sensor\n";
}

void controlMotor()
{
    std::cout << "Calculating motor command\n";
}

void logData()
{
    std::cout << "Recording diagnostic data\n";
}

int main()
{
    readSensor();
    controlMotor();
    logData();

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Code explanation
docs.text:
The program contains three functions:

  • readSensor() represents sensor acquisition.
  • controlMotor() represents motor-control calculations.
  • logData() represents diagnostic logging.

Inside main(), the functions are called sequentially.

The output is:

Reading distance sensor
Calculating motor command
Recording diagnostic data

The execution order is fixed.

The motor-control function cannot begin until readSensor() has returned.

Similarly, logData() cannot begin until controlMotor() has returned.

docs.title: Is sequential programming bad?
docs.text:
No.

Sequential programming is often the simplest & most appropriate/optimal solution for small applications. E.g., a robot that performs one short sensor reading, one calculation & one motor update in a predictable cycle may work well using a sequential program.

However, problems can arise when operations have different execution times or timing requirements.

docs.title: Execution time in a sequential program
docs.text:
From the above example, let's suppose the those three operations take:

Operation Execution time Read sensor 8 ms Calculate motor command 4 ms Record data 12 ms

Assuming the operations execute continuously without interruption and that other overheads are negligible/ignored.

The total execution time is:

\[ C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{sensor}} + C_{\text{control}} + C_{\text{logging}} \]

Substituting the values:

\[ C_{\text{total}} = 8 + 4 + 12 \] \[ \boxed{C_{\text{total}} = 24\ \text{ms}} \]

If the program repeats these operations continuously, one complete cycle requires at least 24 ms under these assumptions.

docs.title: What if motor control requires a 10 ms period?
docs.text:
Suppose the motor controller must execute every 10 ms. A sequential program that performs all three operations once per cycle can't meet that period if the operations require 24 ms in total.

Even though the motor-control calculation itself requires only 4 ms, the other operations delay its next execution.

This is an important distinction:

A task's timing behaviour depends not only on its own execution time, but also on how other activities are organised.

Figure 2.1.1: Illustrative sequential execution on a single processor core. The values represent milliseconds from the beginning of the cycle.

Note

The diagram assumes uninterrupted execution and excludes operating-system scheduling overhead.

Real execution times may vary.

docs.title: C++ example: Simulating sequential task durations
docs.text:
We can use C++ to simulate the time taken by different robot operations.

Create a file named:

sequential_robot.cpp

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <thread>

void readSensor()
{
    std::cout << "Reading sensor...\n";

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(
        std::chrono::milliseconds(8)
    );
}

void controlMotor()
{
    std::cout << "Calculating motor command...\n";

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(
        std::chrono::milliseconds(4)
    );
}

void logData()
{
    std::cout << "Logging data...\n";

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(
        std::chrono::milliseconds(12)
    );
}

int main()
{
    using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

    auto start = Clock::now();

    readSensor();
    controlMotor();
    logData();

    auto finish = Clock::now();

    double elapsed_ms =
        std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(
            finish - start
        ).count();

    std::cout << "Total elapsed time: "
              << elapsed_ms << " ms\n";

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Compile and execute
docs.text:
Using a C++17-compatible GCC compiler:

g++ -std=c++17 -O0 sequential_robot.cpp -o sequential_robot

On Windows PowerShell:

.\sequential_robot.exe

On Linux or macOS:

./sequential_robot

docs.title: Expected behaviour
docs.text:
The program prints messages in the same order as the function calls.

The total elapsed time will normally be approximately 24 ms or longer.

However, the measured duration may vary because of:

  • Operating-system scheduling,
  • Thread wake-up delays,
  • Console output,
  • Other system activities.

Important measurement distinction

std::this_thread::sleep_for() suspends the current thread.

It does not perform CPU-intensive calculations for the requested duration.

Therefore, this example simulates elapsed operation durations, not actual CPU execution times.

The example is intended to demonstrate sequential waiting and timing, not to measure processor workload.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Modify the program so that:

  1. Sensor acquisition takes 5 ms.
  2. Motor control takes 3 ms.
  3. Logging takes 20 ms.

Before running the program, calculate the expected total delay. Run the program five times. Does the measured elapsed time equal exactly 28 ms?

Explain any differences.

docs.title: 2.1.3 What is concurrency?
docs.text:
Concurrency means that multiple activities can make progress during overlapping periods of time.

The activities do not necessarily execute at precisely the same instant.

For example, consider a single-core processor running:

  • Task A: Sensor processing.
  • Task B: Motor control.
  • Task C: Data logging.

The processor might execute a short portion of Task A, switch to Task B, then execute Task C before returning to Task A.

Only one task executes on the processor core at a particular instant, but all three tasks make progress over time.

This is called concurrent execution.

docs.title: Example: A robot performing multiple activities
docs.text:
A mobile robot may need to continue controlling its motors while periodically receiving sensor measurements.

Instead of executing all activities in one long sequential cycle, the program can organise them as separate tasks.

The operating system can then schedule the tasks according to its scheduling policy.

Time  -------------------------------------------------->

CPU    | Sensor | Motor | Logger | Motor | Sensor | Motor |
Figure 2.1.2: Concurrent execution on a single-core processor

The processor executes one task at a time, but switches between tasks.

The tasks are concurrent because their execution progresses over overlapping periods.

Important

Concurrency does not automatically mean that the program runs faster.

Its main benefit is allowing multiple activities to be organised and scheduled independently.

Whether timing performance improves depends on the task design, scheduling policy and hardware. FreeRTOS. RTOS Fundamentals and Task Scheduling. (Read more: RTOS Fundamentals)

docs.title: 2.1.4 Concurrency versus parallelism
docs.text: The terms concurrency and parallelism are related but describe different concepts.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Multiple activities make progress over overlapping periods.

On a single-core processor, this can happen through task switching.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text:
Multiple activities execute simultaneously on different processing resources.

For example, a processor with multiple cores may execute sensor processing on one core and motor control on another at the same instant.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose a robot has two software tasks:

  • Task A processes sensor measurements.
  • Task B calculates motor commands.

On a single-core processor, the operating system may alternate between the tasks.

On a multicore processor, the tasks may execute simultaneously if the scheduler places them on different cores.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Characteristic Concurrency Parallelism Multiple activities can make progress Yes Yes Simultaneous execution required No Yes Possible on a single-core processor Yes Not for two CPU-executing threads simultaneously on the same core Multiple processor cores required No Multiple execution resources are needed for simultaneous CPU execution Main idea Managing overlapping activities Executing activities simultaneously

Remember

Concurrency is about organising multiple activities.

Parallelism is about executing multiple activities at the same time.

A program can be concurrent without being parallel.

Reference: [2].

docs.title: 2.1.5 What is a software task?
docs.text:
In robotics, a task is a logical unit of work that performs a particular function.

Examples include:

  • Reading a distance sensor.
  • Updating a motor controller.
  • Monitoring battery voltage.
  • Processing camera measurements.
  • Recording diagnostic information.

A task may execute:

  • Periodically.
  • In response to an event.
  • Once when requested.

The word task is used somewhat differently across programming environments.

In real-time operating systems such as FreeRTOS, a task is a schedulable execution entity managed by the RTOS.

In general-purpose C++ programming, we can organise logical tasks using functions and execute them through threads.

docs.title: Task versus thread
docs.text:
A task describes the work that needs to be performed.

A thread is an execution mechanism that allows a sequence of instructions to run independently within a process.

For example:

void sensorTask()
{
    // Read and process sensor data.
}

This function represents a logical sensor task.

However, simply defining the function does not create a separate thread.

Calling it normally:

sensorTask();

executes it in the calling thread.

Later, we can create a separate thread using:

std::thread sensorThread(sensorTask);

The sensorTask() function can then execute in the newly created thread.

Note

In C++, std::thread is available from C++11 onwards.

It allows programrs to create separate threads of execution within a process (Read more: std::thread — C++ Reference.).

docs.title: 2.1.6 Periodic and event-driven tasks
docs.text: Robotic software commonly contains both periodic and event-driven activities.

docs.title: Periodic tasks
docs.text:
A periodic task is intended to execute repeatedly at regular intervals.

Examples:

  • Read an encoder every 10 ms.
  • Update motor commands every 20 ms.
  • Monitor battery voltage every 500 ms.

The task period is represented by:

\[ T \]

Its frequency is:

\[ f = \frac{1}{T} \]

For example:

\[ T = 20\ \text{ms} = 0.020\ \text{s} \] \[ f = \frac{1}{0.020} \] \[ \boxed{f = 50\ \text{Hz}} \]

docs.title: Event-driven tasks
docs.text:
An event-driven task executes when a particular event occurs.

Examples:

  • A user presses an emergency-stop button.
  • A new message arrives.
  • A sensor reports that data is available.
  • A communication timeout occurs.

Unlike a periodic task, an event-driven task does not necessarily execute at fixed intervals.

docs.title: Which approach is better?
docs.text:
Neither is universally better. Periodic execution is useful when regular updates are required. Event-driven execution is useful when processing should occur in response to specific events. Many robotic systems use a combination of both. E.g., a motor controller may update periodically, while a communication task waits for incoming commands.

FreeRTOS provides task scheduling and blocking mechanisms that support these types of applications.

Warning

An event-driven design does not automatically provide immediate response.

The event must still be detected and the corresponding task scheduled.

docs.title: 2.1.7 Why not simply use one large loop?
docs.text:
A beginner might organise all robot activities inside a single while loop.

For example:

while (true)
{
    readSensor();
    controlMotor();
    checkBattery();
    logData();
}

This approach is easy to understand.

However, it has several limitations.

docs.title: Limitation 1: Every operation delays the next
docs.text: If logData() takes a long time, the next sensor reading and motor-control calculation are delayed.

docs.title: Limitation 2: Different periods are difficult to manage
docs.text:
Motor control may need to run every 10 ms, while battery monitoring may only be needed every 500 ms.

Calling every function once per loop does not naturally satisfy these different timing requirements.

docs.title: Limitation 3: Blocking operations can delay the entire loop
docs.text:
Suppose readSensor() waits for a sensor response.

While it is waiting, the other functions cannot execute in that same thread.

docs.title: Limitation 4: Timing requirements become harder to analyse
docs.text:
When many activities share one sequential execution path, a delay in one operation affects the timing of the others.

However, it doesn't automatically mean one loop is always unsuitable. A carefully designed single-loop program can be suitable for simple embedded systems. E.g., a cooperative scheduler can use a single loop to execute short operations when their scheduled times arrive.

The important requirement is that operations must not block or execute unpredictably for too long. For more complex applications, separating activities into independently scheduled tasks can make the design easier to organise.

docs.title: C++ example: A simple cooperative task loop
docs.text:
Before introducing multiple threads, we can improve a sequential program by giving different operations their own intended periods.

This example uses a single thread (not multithreaded programming).

Create a file named:

cooperative_robot.cpp

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <thread>

int main()
{
    using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;

    const auto sensor_period =
        std::chrono::milliseconds(50);

    const auto motor_period =
        std::chrono::milliseconds(20);

    auto now = Clock::now();

    auto next_sensor = now;
    auto next_motor = now;

    const auto end_time =
        now + std::chrono::seconds(1);

    while (Clock::now() < end_time)
    {
        now = Clock::now();

        if (now >= next_sensor)
        {
            std::cout << "Sensor update\n";

            next_sensor += sensor_period;
        }

        now = Clock::now();

        if (now >= next_motor)
        {
            std::cout << "Motor update\n";

            next_motor += motor_period;
        }

        std::this_thread::sleep_for(
            std::chrono::milliseconds(1)
        );
    }

    return 0;
}

The program contains two logical activities:

  1. Sensor update every 50 ms.
  2. Motor update every 20 ms.

The variable: next_sensor stores the intended time of the next sensor update.

Similarly next_motor stores the intended time of the next motor update.

The conditions if (now >= next_sensor) and if (now >= next_motor) check whether the corresponding activity is due.

After an activity is executed, its next scheduled time is advanced by one period.

docs.title: Why is this useful?
docs.text: The program does not need to call every function on every iteration. Each logical activity has its own intended period. This is a basic form of cooperative, time-triggered task organisation.

docs.title: Important limitations
docs.text:
The program still uses only one thread.

Therefore:

  • A long sensor operation can delay the motor update.
  • Both activities cannot execute simultaneously.
  • The operating system may delay the loop.
  • The 1 ms sleep can introduce additional timing variation.
  • If the program falls behind schedule, overdue activities may execute in successive loop iterations.

The program is deliberately simple and does not implement a complete overrun-handling policy.

docs.title: 2.1.8 Choosing between sequential and concurrent programming
docs.text:
Concurrency is useful when an application contains activities with different timing requirements or operations that may block independently. However, concurrency introduces additional complexity. E.g., multiple threads may need to access the same sensor data. If they access shared data without appropriate coordination, incorrect or inconsistent results may occur.

These problems are called race conditions and will be studied in later chapters.

docs.title: Practical decision guide
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Identify robot software activities"] --> B{"Can a simple sequential design meet the requirements?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Use a simple sequential design"]
    B -->|"No"| D{"Can short non-blocking operations be scheduled cooperatively?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Consider a cooperative task loop"]
    D -->|"No"| F["Consider independently scheduled threads or RTOS tasks"]
    C --> G["Measure and verify timing"]
    E --> G
    F --> H["Design safe communication and synchronisation"]
    H --> G

The choice should be based on measured timing requirements, system complexity and hardware capabilities.

Do not introduce concurrency merely because it is available.

docs.title: 2.1.9 Example: Selecting an approach for a robot
docs.text:
A small robot performs the following activities:

Activity Period Typical processing duration Read distance sensor 50 ms 5 ms Calculate motor command 20 ms 3 ms Record diagnostic data 500 ms 15 ms

Suppose all three functions are executed sequentially in one repeated cycle.

The combined processing duration is:

\[ C_{\text{total}} = 5 + 3 + 15 \] \[ \boxed{C_{\text{total}} = 23\ \text{ms}} \]

If every activity executes once per cycle, the motor-control function cannot achieve a 20 ms start-to-start period in this design.

docs.title: Possible improvement 1: Cooperative scheduling
docs.text:
Execute the functions only when their intended periods are reached.

This may be sufficient if:

  • All operations are short.
  • Operations do not block unpredictably.
  • The resulting timing measurements satisfy the requirements.

docs.title: Possible improvement 2: Separate threads
docs.text:
Use independently scheduled threads for:

  • Sensor acquisition.
  • Motor control.
  • Logging.

This allows the operating system to schedule the activities separately.

However, shared data must be handled safely.

docs.title: Which solution should we choose?
docs.text:
There is not enough information to guarantee that either approach will satisfy every deadline.

We would need to know:

  • Worst-case execution times.
  • Deadlines.
  • Blocking behaviour.
  • Scheduling policy.
  • Hardware and operating-system characteristics.

The appropriate engineering approach is to implement a suitable design, measure its behaviour, and assess whether the timing requirements are satisfied. For strict timing guarantees, additional analysis, and validation may be required.
